definition: To deliberately avoid or stay away from something, often on principle.
example: Many seasoned hikers eschew paved trails, preferring rough paths that few others take.
nuance: Unlike simply avoiding, eschewing implies a deliberate, often principled choice to do without something.
prompt: A chef designs a new menu around simple, fresh ingredients.
options: The chef chose to eschew heavy sauces so the vegetables could speak for themselves.
The chef asked diners to eschew each mouthful slowly to savor the herbs.
To eschew butter, the chef added an extra spoonful of it to every dish.
Stuck behind a stalled bus, the chef was forced to eschew the morning farmers' market.
reasons: Deliberately leaving out rich sauces for the sake of a principle fits the word exactly.
This confuses the word with chewing; it has nothing to do with biting food.
Using more of something is the reverse of steering clear of it.
Missing something because of traffic is an accident, not a willing choice to avoid it.

practice.prompt: A student revising a research paper wants it to read clearly.
options: In her introduction, she eschewed the theory loudly and urged readers to adopt it.
She eschewed the submission deadline simply because the due date slipped her mind.
She decided to eschew jargon and explain each idea in plain, everyday words.
She eschewed the eraser end of her pencil while staring at the blank screen.
reasons: Championing an idea is espousing it, which is the opposite of turning away from it.
Forgetting something is not a deliberate decision to keep away from it.
Purposely giving up technical terms to make the writing clearer is a fitting use.
Gnawing on a pencil is chewing; the word is about avoidance, not biting.
